title: EU Law
topics: Free movement of persons and citizenship
EU law in the UK after Brexit

notes.h: The EU institutions and how EU law is made
notes.body:
The EU can act only within the competences the Member States have conferred on it (Art 5 TEU). In shared competences it must also respect subsidiarity and proportionality; national parliaments police subsidiarity through the yellow and orange card procedures in Protocol No 2.

The seven institutions (Art 13 TEU):
- European Parliament: directly elected; co-legislator and budgetary authority with the Council; elects the Commission President and can censure the Commission (Art 234 TFEU).
- European Council: heads of state or government; sets political direction but does not legislate (Art 15 TEU).
- Council: one minister per state; co-legislator. Qualified majority means 55% of states representing at least 65% of the EU population; a blocking minority needs at least four states (Art 16 TEU).
- Commission: independent; near-monopoly of legislative initiative; guardian of the Treaties (Art 17 TEU).
- Court of Justice of the EU (the Court of Justice and the General Court), the European Central Bank and the Court of Auditors.

Legal acts (Art 288 TFEU): regulations are binding in their entirety and directly applicable; directives bind as to the result to be achieved, leaving form and methods to the state; decisions bind addressees; recommendations and opinions do not bind. Delegated acts (Art 290) amend or supplement non-essential elements; implementing acts (Art 291) secure uniform implementation.

The ordinary legislative procedure (Art 294 TFEU): Commission proposal; Parliament's first-reading position; the Council approves it or adopts its own position; Parliament's second reading, where rejection or amendment needs an absolute majority of component members; then conciliation and a third reading. Most files close at first reading after informal trilogues. Special procedures give Parliament only consent or consultation, and consultation is an essential procedural requirement (Roquette Frères (Isoglucose), 1980).

Legal basis matters. Art 114 TFEU cannot support a measure that does not genuinely improve the internal market (Germany v Parliament and Council (Tobacco Advertising), 2000). Art 352 is a residual clause requiring unanimity.

Illustration: a directive on e-cigarette labelling rests on Art 114. The Court asks whether it removes real obstacles to trade or appreciable distortions of competition; a health motive does not invalidate it if so.

Common pitfalls:
- Confusing the European Council, the Council and the Council of Europe (a separate body behind the ECHR).
- Saying the Commission adopts legislation: it proposes; Parliament and Council adopt.
- Ignoring institutional balance: Parliament may sue to protect its prerogatives (Chernobyl, 1990).

notes.h: Sources of EU law, supremacy and direct effect
notes.body:
Primary law comprises the TEU, the TFEU, the Charter of Fundamental Rights (equal in value to the Treaties, Art 6(1) TEU) and the general principles. EU international agreements bind the institutions and Member States (Art 216(2) TFEU). Secondary legislation sits below.

Supremacy is a judicial creation, noted in Declaration 17 to the Lisbon Treaty.
- Costa v ENEL (1964): states have limited their sovereign rights, so later national law cannot override EU law.
- Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (1970): EU law prevails even over national constitutions.
- Simmenthal (1978): every national court must disapply conflicting national law of its own motion.
- Factortame (1990): courts must be able to grant interim relief to protect EU rights, even against an Act of Parliament.

Some national courts accept primacy conditionally: the German Constitutional Court's Solange line and its 2020 Weiss (PSPP) ruling, and the Polish Constitutional Tribunal's 2021 rejection of primacy (K 3/21).

Direct effect lets individuals rely on EU law in national courts. Van Gend en Loos (1963): the provision must be clear, precise and unconditional.
- Treaty articles can be effective vertically and horizontally (Defrenne (No 2), 1976; Angonese, 2000).
- Regulations are generally directly effective both ways.
- Directives are effective only after the transposition deadline (Ratti, 1979) and only vertically (Marshall, 1986; Faccini Dori, 1994). "The state" is read broadly: Foster v British Gas (1990), clarified in Farrell v Whitty (2017), covers bodies given a public-interest task and special powers.
- Some general principles and Charter rights bind private parties: non-discrimination (Mangold, 2005; Kücükdeveci, 2010; Egenberger, 2018) and paid annual leave (Bauer, 2018). Art 27 on worker consultation did not qualify (Association de médiation sociale, 2014).

Worked example: a directive requiring extra paid leave is not transposed by its deadline. Ana, a nurse at a public hospital, can rely on it against her employer as an emanation of the state. Ben, at a private firm, cannot; he must use indirect effect, a horizontally effective Charter right, or state liability.

Common pitfalls:
- Treating "directly applicable" (no national implementation needed) as the same as "directly effective" (creates enforceable rights).
- Claiming directives have horizontal direct effect.
- Forgetting that the Charter binds Member States only when implementing EU law (Art 51(1); Åkerberg Fransson, 2013).

notes.h: Indirect effect, incidental effect and state liability
notes.body:
Because directives lack horizontal direct effect, the Court built further routes, grounded in sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU).

Indirect effect (consistent interpretation):
- Von Colson (1984): courts must interpret national law in light of a directive's wording and purpose.
- Marleasing (1990): this applies whether the national law came before or after the directive, and between private parties.
- Pfeiffer (2004): courts must consider the whole of national law and every recognised interpretive method.
- Adeneler (2006): the full duty starts when the transposition period ends.

Limits: no interpretation contra legem (Pupino, 2005; Dominguez, 2012); legal certainty; and a directive cannot by itself create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen, 1987). UK courts sometimes read words into statutes to achieve conformity (Litster v Forth Dry Dock, 1989).

Incidental effect: in CIA Security (1996) and Unilever Italia (2000), unnotified national technical rules were unenforceable even between private parties. The directive imposed no obligation on anyone; it removed a defence resting on unlawful national law.

State liability began with Francovich (1991). Brasserie du Pêcheur and Factortame (No 3) (1996) set the conditions:
- the rule must be intended to confer rights on individuals;
- the breach must be sufficiently serious, a manifest and grave disregard of the limits on the state's discretion;
- a direct causal link between breach and loss.

Factors include the clarity of the rule, the discretion left, intention, excusable error, and positions taken by EU institutions. Non-transposition is serious per se (Dillenkofer, 1996). With little or no discretion, mere infringement may suffice (Hedley Lomas, 1996). A good-faith reading of an unclear directive may be excusable (ex p British Telecommunications, 1996). Liability extends to last-instance courts for manifest breaches (Köbler, 2003), and national law cannot limit it to intent or gross negligence (Traghetti, 2006). Procedure follows national rules subject to equivalence and effectiveness.

Worked example: State Z never transposes a directive requiring insolvency protection for package holidays. When an operator collapses, stranded travellers can sue Z: the directive confers identifiable rights, non-transposition is serious per se, and the loss flows directly from it (the Dillenkofer facts).

Common pitfalls:
- Treating indirect effect as automatic: it depends on whether the national wording can bear the meaning.
- Reciting the Francovich conditions without the Brasserie refinement.
- Forgetting the criminal-liability limit.

notes.h: Preliminary references, infringement actions and judicial review
notes.body:
Art 267 TFEU lets national courts ask the Court of Justice about the interpretation of the Treaties and the validity and interpretation of EU acts. The Court interprets; the national court applies the ruling.

- "Court or tribunal" is an EU concept: established by law, permanent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes procedure, applies rules of law, independent (Dorsch Consult, 1997).
- Lower courts may refer even when bound by a higher court's view (Rheinmühlen, 1974; Elchinov, 2010).
- Courts with no judicial remedy against their decisions must refer (Art 267(3)), judged concretely: a court whose decisions can be appealed with leave is not last-instance (Lyckeskog, 2002).
- CILFIT (1982) exceptions: the question is irrelevant, already answered (acte éclairé), or leaves no reasonable doubt (acte clair). Consorzio Italian Management (2021) requires the answer to be equally obvious to other national courts and to the Court of Justice.
- Only the Court can invalidate EU acts (Foto-Frost, 1987), though national courts may grant interim relief meanwhile (Zuckerfabrik, 1991).
- Hypothetical or contrived questions are refused (Foglia v Novello, 1980).
- Since 1 October 2024 the General Court hears references on VAT, excise duties, the Customs Code, tariff classification, passenger compensation and assistance, and emissions trading.

Infringement proceedings (Arts 258-260 TFEU):
- Letter of formal notice, reasoned opinion, then referral to the Court; the Commission has a discretion (Star Fruit, 1989).
- Internal difficulties and reciprocity are no defence (Commission v Luxembourg and Belgium, 1964).
- Art 260(2) allows a lump sum and periodic penalty together for ignoring a judgment (Commission v France, 2005); Art 260(3) allows penalties in the first judgment for failure to notify transposition.
- Interim orders under Art 279 can carry daily penalties, as against Poland in 2021 over judicial independence.

Judicial review (Art 263 TFEU): non-privileged applicants must be addressees, directly and individually concerned (Plaumann, 1963), or challenging a regulatory act of direct concern that entails no implementing measures. A regulatory act is a non-legislative act of general application (Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2013). The time limit is two months.

Worked example: Spain's supreme court is unsure whether a VAT exemption covers online tutoring. It must refer unless a CILFIT exception applies. The reference is lodged with the Court of Justice, which transfers it to the General Court because it concerns VAT.

Common pitfalls:
- Saying the Court of Justice decides the case.
- Treating acte clair as easy: failure to refer can found Köbler liability or an infringement action (Commission v France, 2018).

Three sets of rules must be kept apart.

1. Customs duties and charges having equivalent effect (Arts 28 and 30 TFEU). Any charge levied because goods cross a border is banned, whatever its size or purpose (Statistical Levy, 1969; Diamantarbeiders, 1969). Exceptions: payment for a genuine, proportionate service to the trader, or inspections required by EU law.

2. Internal taxation (Art 110). Art 110(1) bans taxing imports more heavily than similar domestic products (Humblot, 1985). Art 110(2) bans taxes protecting competing products (Commission v UK (wine and beer), 1983). Arts 30 and 110 are mutually exclusive.

3. Quantitative restrictions and measures having equivalent effect (MEQRs) (Arts 34-36).
- Dassonville (1974): all trading rules capable of hindering intra-EU trade, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially.
- Distinctly applicable measures discriminate openly (Buy Irish, 1982). Failing to stop private blockades can breach Art 34 (Spanish strawberries, 1997).
- Cassis de Dijon (1979): equally applicable rules can still breach Art 34. Goods lawfully marketed in one state should be admitted elsewhere (mutual recognition) unless a mandatory requirement justifies the rule: consumer protection, fair trading, public health, fiscal supervision, the environment (Danish bottles, 1988), fundamental rights (Schmidberger, 2003).
- Keck (1993): selling arrangements fall outside Art 34 if they apply to all traders and affect domestic and imported goods alike in law and in fact. Advertising or online-sales bans may fail the factual limb (Gourmet, 2001; DocMorris, 2003).
- Italian trailers (2009) and Mickelsson and Roos (2009) add a market-access test for rules on product use.
- Exports (Art 35): Groenveld (1979) required discrimination; Gysbrechts (2008) caught a rule with greater practical effect on exports.

Justification: Art 36 covers public morality, policy and security, health and life, national treasures, and industrial property. Economic aims never qualify. Measures must be proportionate and not disguised restrictions (Conegate, 1986, contrasted with Henn and Darby, 1979). In Scotch Whisky Association (2015) the Court of Justice left proportionality of minimum alcohol pricing to national courts; the UK Supreme Court upheld it in 2017.

Worked example: State Y bans energy drinks above a caffeine threshold. This is a product rule, so Keck does not apply. Y must show a genuine health risk on scientific evidence and that labelling would not suffice.

Common pitfalls:
- Applying Keck to rules on the product itself (composition, packaging, labelling).
- Relying on economic justifications.
- Confusing a border charge with internal taxation.

notes.h: Free movement of workers and EU citizenship
notes.body:
Workers (Art 45 TFEU). A worker performs services for and under the direction of another for remuneration (Lawrie-Blum, 1986). Work must be genuine and effective, not marginal and ancillary; part-time counts (Levin, 1982), even if topped up by benefits (Kempf, 1986), but mainly rehabilitative work may not (Bettray, 1989). Jobseekers are protected while they have genuine chances of work (Antonissen, 1991). Regulation 492/2011, Art 7(2), gives equal social and tax advantages.

Art 45 catches direct and indirect discrimination and non-discriminatory obstacles to market access (Bosman, 1995), and binds private parties (Angonese, 2000). Exceptions: public policy, security and health (Art 45(3)); public service posts involving public power (Art 45(4); Commission v Belgium, 1980).

Citizenship (Arts 20-21 TFEU) and Directive 2004/38:
- Art 6: residence up to three months with an identity document.
- Art 7: beyond three months for workers and the self-employed, the self-sufficient with comprehensive sickness insurance, and students. Art 7(3) retains worker status, for example after involuntary unemployment.
- Art 16: permanent residence after five years' continuous legal residence.
- Family members (Art 2(2)) include spouses, registered partners, descendants under 21 or dependent, and dependent ascendants. No prior lawful residence elsewhere is required (Metock, 2008); a same-sex spouse married abroad counts (Coman, 2018).
- Art 24 allows refusal of social assistance in the first three months and to jobseekers, and of student maintenance aid to the inactive before permanent residence.

The case law has moved from generosity (Grzelczyk, 2001; Baumbast, 2002) to caution: Dano (2014), Alimanovic (2015) and Commission v UK (2016) allow refusal of benefits to those without a right to reside.

Expulsion (Arts 27-28): personal conduct must be a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental interest of society (Bouchereau, 1977). Permanent residents need serious grounds; ten-year residents and minors need imperative grounds of public security (Tsakouridis, 2010).

Zambrano (2011) protects the substance of citizenship: a third-country parent of EU-citizen children cannot be removed if the children would have to leave the EU. It was narrowed in McCarthy and Dereci (2011) and refined in Chavez-Vilchez (2017).

Worked example: Marta, a Spanish national, works 12 hours a week in a Lyon bakery. Her work is genuine and effective, so she is a worker (Levin, Kempf) and can claim French social advantages equally.

Common pitfalls:
- Assuming inactive citizens can always claim benefits after Grzelczyk.
- Forgetting Art 28's graduated protection against expulsion.

notes.h: Establishment, services and the basics of competition law
notes.body:
Establishment (Art 49 TFEU) is a stable and continuous economic activity from a fixed base in another state; services (Arts 56-57) are temporary and cross-border, for remuneration. Gebhard (1995) distinguishes them by duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity.

- Reyners (1974) and Van Binsbergen (1974) gave both freedoms direct effect.
- Gebhard test for restrictions: non-discriminatory, justified by imperative requirements in the general interest, suitable, and no more than necessary.
- Companies (Art 54): registering where rules are lightest and trading through a branch elsewhere is lawful (Centros, 1999); legal capacity must be recognised (Überseering, 2002). A state may stop a company moving its seat while keeping its law (Cartesio, 2008), but cross-border conversion is protected (Polbud, 2017).
- Services: Säger (1991) catches non-discriminatory rules liable to impede services; Alpine Investments (1995) caught an export restriction. Recipients are protected (Luisi and Carbone, 1984), including patients (Kohll, 1998; Watts, 2006).
- Union collective action is a restriction needing justification (Viking, 2007; Laval, 2007).

Competition law applies to undertakings: any entity engaged in economic activity, whatever its status or financing (Höfner and Elser, 1991).

Art 101 TFEU prohibits agreements, decisions of associations and concerted practices that may affect inter-state trade and have as their object or effect the restriction of competition.
- Object restrictions reveal sufficient harm on their face, such as price-fixing or market-sharing (Cartes Bancaires, 2014); others need effects analysis.
- Agreements must be appreciable (Völk, 1969), but object restrictions are appreciable by nature (Expedia, 2012).
- Infringing agreements are void (Art 101(2)) unless they meet Art 101(3): efficiencies, a fair share for consumers, indispensable restrictions, no elimination of competition. This applies directly under Regulation 1/2003, and block exemptions such as Regulation 2022/720 on vertical agreements give safe harbours.

Art 102 prohibits abuse of a dominant position: power to behave appreciably independently of competitors and customers (United Brands, 1978). A share of 50% or more raises a presumption (AKZO, 1991). Abuses include excessive and predatory pricing, loyalty rebates (Hoffmann-La Roche, 1979; Intel, 2017), refusal of access to indispensable facilities (Bronner, 1998) and self-preferencing (Google Shopping, 2024). Fines reach up to 10% of worldwide turnover.

Worked example: three cement producers agree to keep out of each other's regions. This is market-sharing, an object restriction, so no effects analysis is needed and Art 101(3) is realistically unavailable.

Common pitfalls:
- Confusing establishment with services.
- Treating market share alone as proof of dominance.
- Saying dominance is unlawful: only abuse is.

notes.h: EU law in the UK after Brexit
notes.body:
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020. EU law continued to apply under the Withdrawal Agreement until the implementation period ended on 31 December 2020.

Legislation:
- The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (EUWA) repealed the European Communities Act 1972 and converted EU law into "retained EU law": EU-derived domestic legislation, direct EU legislation and directly effective rights. It kept supremacy for pre-exit law, excluded the Charter (s 5(4)) and ended Francovich damages.
- The European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020 implemented the Withdrawal Agreement; s 7A EUWA gives it effect and priority.
- The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 revoked listed instruments and, from 1 January 2024, renamed the remainder "assimilated law". It abolished supremacy and the general principles, ended directly effective rights under s 4 EUWA, and gave ministers powers to restate, revoke or replace assimilated law.

Courts. Pre-2021 CJEU case law, called "assimilated case law" since 2024 (previously retained case law), binds lower courts, but the Supreme Court and some appellate courts, including the Court of Appeal, may depart from it. The 2023 Act revised the departure test and lets lower courts refer points on it upwards. The Court of Appeal set out its cautious approach in TuneIn v Warner Music (2021). New CJEU rulings do not bind, though courts may have regard to them.

Withdrawal Agreement. Part Two protects residence rights of EU citizens in the UK and UK nationals in the EU as at the end of the implementation period. UK courts may refer citizens' rights questions to the CJEU for eight years after that date; the Independent Monitoring Authority oversees compliance.

Northern Ireland. The Protocol, revised by the 2023 Windsor Framework, keeps Northern Ireland aligned with many EU goods rules, with continuing CJEU jurisdiction and a "Stormont Brake" on amended rules. Art 2 prevents diminution of certain Belfast/Good Friday Agreement rights; in Dillon (2024) the Northern Ireland High Court, upheld by the Court of Appeal, used it, via s 7A EUWA, to disapply the Legacy Act 2023's immunity provisions. The Supreme Court allowed the Government's appeal and set those disapplication declarations aside (Re Dillon [2026] UKSC 15, 7 May 2026). It accepted that Art 2 can have direct effect in limited circumstances, such as alongside the equality directives in Annex 1, but found no directly effective EU right that the immunity scheme breached. The High Court's separate Human Rights Act declarations of incompatibility on immunity were not appealed and remain in force. In Allister (2023) the Supreme Court upheld the Protocol, holding that s 7A had modified the Acts of Union.

The Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2020) gives the CJEU no role and excludes direct effect for private parties.

Worked example: in 2026 a claimant relies on a general principle of EU law to challenge a 2019 regulation implementing a directive. The argument fails because general principles ceased to be part of domestic law from 2024; the claimant must rely on the assimilated text, domestic public law or the Human Rights Act 1998.

Common pitfalls:
- Saying "retained EU law" for the post-2023 position instead of "assimilated law".
- Assuming CJEU case law no longer matters: assimilated case law binds lower courts, and the Windsor Framework keeps live CJEU jurisdiction.

cards.f: What is the principle of conferral?
cards.b: The EU may act only within the limits of the competences the Member States have conferred on it in the Treaties; competences not conferred remain with the states (Art 5(2) TEU).

cards.f: Define qualified majority voting in the Council.
cards.b: At least 55% of Member States, representing at least 65% of the EU population. A blocking minority must include at least four Member States (Art 16(4) TEU).

cards.f: Which institution holds the near-monopoly of legislative initiative?
cards.b: The European Commission (Art 17(2) TEU). Parliament and the Council can request proposals but cannot normally table them themselves.

cards.f: Distinguish the European Council from the Council.
cards.b: The European Council gathers heads of state or government to set political direction and does not legislate. The Council (of Ministers) is a co-legislator made up of national ministers.

cards.f: How does a regulation differ from a directive under Art 288 TFEU?
cards.b: A regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States. A directive binds as to the result to be achieved but leaves the choice of form and methods to national authorities.

cards.f: What did Tobacco Advertising (2000) decide about Art 114 TFEU?
cards.b: Art 114 is not a general power to regulate the internal market. A measure based on it must genuinely improve the conditions for the internal market, so a near-total advertising ban was annulled.

cards.f: Why was the Isoglucose case (Roquette Frères, 1980) important?
cards.b: The Council adopted a regulation before Parliament had given its required opinion. The Court annulled it, treating consultation as an essential procedural requirement reflecting democratic participation.

cards.f: What is the yellow card procedure?
cards.b: Under Protocol No 2, if national parliaments with at least one third of the allocated votes object that a draft breaches subsidiarity, the draft must be reviewed. It can then be maintained, amended or withdrawn.

cards.f: Distinguish delegated acts from implementing acts.
cards.b: Delegated acts (Art 290 TFEU) supplement or amend non-essential elements of a legislative act. Implementing acts (Art 291) set uniform conditions for implementing binding acts and are adopted by the Commission under committee control.

cards.f: What majority does Parliament need to reject or amend the Council's position at second reading?
cards.b: An absolute majority of its component members, not just of those voting (Art 294(7) TFEU).

cards.f: State the Van Gend en Loos (1963) test for direct effect.
cards.b: The provision must be sufficiently clear, precise and unconditional. The Court described the Community as a new legal order whose subjects include individuals as well as states.

cards.f: What did Costa v ENEL (1964) establish?
cards.b: The primacy of EU law over later national legislation, because Member States had limited their sovereign rights by joining.

cards.f: What duty did Simmenthal (1978) place on national courts?
cards.b: Every national court must disapply conflicting national law of its own motion, without waiting for the legislature or a constitutional court to set it aside.

cards.f: Can directives have horizontal direct effect?
cards.b: No. Marshall (1986) and Faccini Dori (1994) confirm that directives can be relied on only against the state or its emanations.

cards.f: When can a directive first be directly effective?
cards.b: Only once its transposition deadline has passed (Ratti, 1979).

cards.f: What test identifies an emanation of the state after Farrell v Whitty (2017)?
cards.b: A body entrusted by the state with a public-interest task and given special powers for that purpose. The Foster v British Gas criteria are not cumulative.

cards.f: Which case gave a Treaty article horizontal direct effect on equal pay?
cards.b: Defrenne v Sabena (No 2) (1976), on what is now Art 157 TFEU.

cards.f: How did Mangold (2005) and Kücükdeveci (2010) get around the bar on horizontal direct effect?
cards.b: They treated non-discrimination on grounds of age as a general principle of EU law, given expression by the directive, which national courts must apply even between private parties.

cards.f: When does the Charter bind Member States?
cards.b: Only when they are implementing EU law (Art 51(1)), which Åkerberg Fransson (2013) read as acting within the scope of EU law.

cards.f: Which Charter right was held capable of horizontal effect in Bauer (2018)?
cards.b: The right to paid annual leave in Art 31(2), allowing heirs to claim payment in lieu from a private employer.

cards.f: What is indirect effect?
cards.b: The duty on national courts to interpret national law, as far as possible, in conformity with a directive's wording and purpose (Von Colson, 1984; Marleasing, 1990).

cards.f: What did Marleasing (1990) add to Von Colson?
cards.b: The duty applies whether the national law came before or after the directive, and it applies in proceedings between private parties.

cards.f: Name two limits on consistent interpretation.
cards.b: It cannot require an interpretation contra legem (Pupino, 2005; Dominguez, 2012), and a directive cannot by itself create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen, 1987).

cards.f: What is meant by incidental horizontal effect?
cards.b: A directive is used to exclude conflicting national law in a dispute between private parties, without itself imposing obligations, as in CIA Security (1996) and Unilever Italia (2000).

cards.f: List the Brasserie du Pêcheur (1996) conditions for state liability.
cards.b: The rule breached must confer rights on individuals; the breach must be sufficiently serious; and there must be a direct causal link between breach and damage.

cards.f: What makes a breach 'sufficiently serious'?
cards.b: A manifest and grave disregard by the state of the limits on its discretion. Factors include the clarity of the rule, the discretion left, intention, excusability of any error and the stance of EU institutions.

cards.f: What did Dillenkofer (1996) decide?
cards.b: Failure to take any measures to transpose a directive within the deadline is in itself a sufficiently serious breach.

cards.f: Why did the UK escape liability in ex p British Telecommunications (1996)?
cards.b: The directive was imprecisely worded and the UK's reading was made in good faith and shared by other states, so the error was excusable and the breach not sufficiently serious.

cards.f: What did Köbler (2003) add to state liability?
cards.b: A state can be liable for a manifest infringement of EU law by a court adjudicating at last instance.

cards.f: When does the full duty of consistent interpretation start?
cards.b: When the transposition period expires (Adeneler, 2006). Before then, courts must avoid interpretations that would seriously compromise the directive's aims.

cards.f: What may the Court of Justice rule on under Art 267 TFEU?
cards.b: The interpretation of the Treaties, and the validity and interpretation of acts of EU institutions, bodies, offices or agencies.

cards.f: List the CILFIT (1982) exceptions to the duty to refer.
cards.b: The question is irrelevant; the Court has already answered it (acte éclairé); or the answer is so obvious that there is no reasonable doubt (acte clair).

cards.f: What did Foto-Frost (1987) decide?
cards.b: National courts may reject a challenge to the validity of an EU act but cannot themselves declare it invalid; only the Court of Justice can.

cards.f: Which factors from Dorsch Consult (1997) identify a 'court or tribunal'?
cards.b: Established by law, permanent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes procedure, applies rules of law, and independent.

cards.f: What are the stages of an Art 258 TFEU infringement action?
cards.b: A letter of formal notice, a reasoned opinion with a deadline for compliance, and then referral to the Court of Justice.

cards.f: Can the Commission be forced to bring infringement proceedings?
cards.b: No. It has a discretion, and an individual cannot challenge its refusal to act (Star Fruit, 1989).

cards.f: What does Art 260(3) TFEU allow?
cards.b: Financial penalties in the first infringement judgment where a state has failed to notify measures transposing a legislative directive.

cards.f: What is the Plaumann (1963) test for individual concern?
cards.b: An applicant must be affected by reason of attributes peculiar to it, or circumstances differentiating it from all other persons, as if it were an addressee.

cards.f: Which preliminary references has the General Court heard since 1 October 2024?
cards.b: References in specified areas: VAT, excise duties, the Customs Code, tariff classification, passenger compensation and assistance, and the emissions trading scheme.

cards.f: What did Consorzio Italian Management (2021) add to CILFIT?
cards.b: A last-instance court relying on acte clair must be convinced the answer is equally obvious to other national courts and the Court of Justice; divergent national case law is a warning sign.

cards.f: State the Dassonville (1974) formula.
cards.b: All trading rules enacted by Member States capable of hindering, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially, intra-EU trade are measures having equivalent effect to quantitative restrictions.

cards.f: What principle did Cassis de Dijon (1979) establish?
cards.b: Mutual recognition: goods lawfully produced and marketed in one state should in principle be admitted to others, unless an equally applicable rule is justified by a mandatory requirement.

cards.f: What are selling arrangements under Keck (1993)?
cards.b: Rules on how, where, when and by whom goods are sold. They fall outside Art 34 if they apply to all traders and affect domestic and imported products alike in law and in fact.

cards.f: Why did the advertising ban in Gourmet (2001) still breach Art 34?
cards.b: For products like alcohol, which consumers know through familiarity with local products, a total ban on advertising hit imports harder in fact, so it failed the second Keck condition.

cards.f: Can a purely economic aim justify a restriction on goods?
cards.b: No. Economic objectives such as protecting domestic industry are never accepted under Art 36 or the mandatory requirements.

cards.f: Distinguish Art 30 from Art 110 TFEU.
cards.b: Art 30 bans charges imposed because goods cross a border. Art 110 bans discriminatory or protective internal taxation. They are mutually exclusive.

cards.f: What did the Italian trailers case (2009) add?
cards.b: A market access test: a rule that hinders access to the market for imported products, such as a ban on using motorcycles with trailers, is an MEQR even if not a selling arrangement or product rule.

cards.f: How did Gysbrechts (2008) change the approach to Art 35?
cards.b: It moved beyond Groenveld's requirement of discrimination, catching a ban on taking payment details before the end of a withdrawal period because it affected exports more in fact.

cards.f: Compare Henn and Darby (1979) with Conegate (1986).
cards.b: In Henn and Darby, a UK ban on obscene imports was justified on public morality because similar domestic goods were also restricted. In Conegate it failed because the UK did not prohibit equivalent domestic goods.

cards.f: Can a state's inaction breach Art 34?
cards.b: Yes. France breached Art 34 with Art 4(3) TEU by failing to take adequate measures against farmers' violent blockades of imported produce (Commission v France, 1997).

cards.f: Define a worker under Art 45 TFEU.
cards.b: Someone who, for a period, performs services for and under the direction of another in return for remuneration (Lawrie-Blum, 1986).

cards.f: Does part-time work qualify for worker status?
cards.b: Yes, if genuine and effective rather than marginal and ancillary (Levin, 1982), even if income is supplemented by public funds (Kempf, 1986).

cards.f: What rights do jobseekers have?
cards.b: A right to reside while seeking work for a reasonable period while they have genuine chances of being engaged (Antonissen, 1991), but host states may refuse social assistance (Art 24(2) Directive 2004/38).

cards.f: When is permanent residence acquired?
cards.b: After five years of continuous legal residence in the host state (Art 16 Directive 2004/38).

cards.f: What conditions apply to economically inactive citizens residing beyond three months?
cards.b: Sufficient resources not to become a burden on the host state's social assistance system and comprehensive sickness insurance (Art 7(1)(b) Directive 2004/38).

cards.f: What did Dano (2014) decide?
cards.b: An economically inactive citizen without sufficient resources, and so without a right to reside under the Directive, could be refused special non-contributory benefits on equal-treatment grounds.

cards.f: State the threshold for expulsion on public policy grounds.
cards.b: The individual's personal conduct must be a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting a fundamental interest of society (Bouchereau, 1977; Art 27(2) Directive 2004/38).

cards.f: What is the Zambrano (2011) principle?
cards.b: A Member State cannot deprive EU-citizen children of the genuine enjoyment of the substance of their citizenship rights, for example by removing a third-country parent on whom they depend.

cards.f: What does Art 45(4) TFEU exclude, and how narrowly?
cards.b: Employment in the public service. It covers only posts involving participation in public power and safeguarding the general interests of the state (Commission v Belgium, 1980).

cards.f: What did Metock (2008) decide?
cards.b: A host state cannot require a third-country family member to have previously resided lawfully in another Member State before benefiting from Directive 2004/38.

cards.f: How does Gebhard (1995) distinguish establishment from services?
cards.b: By the duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity of the activity. Having some infrastructure in the host state does not by itself mean establishment.

cards.f: State the Gebhard four-part test for restrictions.
cards.b: Non-discriminatory application, justification by imperative requirements in the general interest, suitability for the aim, and no more than necessary to attain it.

cards.f: What did Centros (1999) decide?
cards.b: Registering a company in a state with lighter rules in order to trade through a branch elsewhere is a use of freedom of establishment, not an abuse in itself.

cards.f: What is an undertaking in EU competition law?
cards.b: Any entity engaged in an economic activity, regardless of legal status and how it is financed (Höfner and Elser, 1991).

cards.f: What are the four conditions in Art 101(3) TFEU?
cards.b: The agreement improves production or distribution or promotes progress; consumers get a fair share of the benefit; restrictions are indispensable; and competition is not eliminated for a substantial part of the products.

cards.f: What is a restriction 'by object'?
cards.b: A type of coordination revealing a sufficient degree of harm to competition on its face, such as price-fixing or market-sharing, so effects need not be shown (Cartes Bancaires, 2014).

cards.f: How did United Brands (1978) define dominance?
cards.b: A position of economic strength enabling an undertaking to prevent effective competition by behaving to an appreciable extent independently of competitors, customers and consumers.

cards.f: What market share raises a presumption of dominance?
cards.b: A share of 50% or more, absent exceptional circumstances (AKZO, 1991).

cards.f: What are the Bronner (1998) conditions for refusal to supply?
cards.b: Refusal must be likely to eliminate all competition from the requester, be incapable of objective justification, and the facility must be indispensable with no actual or potential substitute.

cards.f: What did Viking and Laval (2007) decide about trade union action?
cards.b: Collective action can restrict freedom of establishment or services; the right to strike is a fundamental right but the action must still be justified and proportionate.

cards.f: What happened on 31 December 2020?
cards.b: The implementation period ended (IP completion day). EU law stopped applying in the UK as such, and retained EU law took effect.

cards.f: What is 'assimilated law'?
cards.b: The name, from 1 January 2024, for the remaining body of retained EU law, under the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023.

cards.f: What did the 2023 Act do to supremacy and general principles?
cards.b: It abolished the supremacy of retained EU law and removed the general principles of EU law from domestic law, for the period after 2023.

cards.f: Which courts may depart from assimilated (formerly retained) CJEU case law?
cards.b: The Supreme Court and certain appellate courts, including the Court of Appeal, the Inner House of the Court of Session and the High Court of Justiciary. Lower courts remain bound.

cards.f: Did the Charter survive in UK law after Brexit?
cards.b: No. s 5(4) of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 provided that the Charter is not part of domestic law after exit.

cards.f: What does s 7A EUWA do?
cards.b: It gives domestic effect to rights and obligations arising under the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Windsor Framework, and gives them priority over inconsistent domestic law.

cards.f: What is the Stormont Brake?
cards.b: A Windsor Framework mechanism allowing members of the Northern Ireland Assembly to trigger a process that can stop amended EU goods rules from applying in Northern Ireland.

cards.f: What did the Supreme Court decide in Allister (2023)?
cards.b: The Northern Ireland Protocol was lawful: s 7A EUWA had validly modified the trade provisions of the Acts of Union, and Parliament's intention was clear.

cards.f: For how long can UK courts refer citizens' rights questions to the CJEU?
cards.b: For eight years after the end of the implementation period, under Art 158 of the Withdrawal Agreement.

cards.f: Does the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement have direct effect?
cards.b: No. It expressly excludes the creation of rights or obligations for persons that can be invoked directly in domestic law.

questions.q: Which institution adopts legislation jointly with the European Parliament under the ordinary legislative procedure?
options: The European Council
The Council of the European Union
The European Commission
The Council of Europe
questions.why: The Council (of ministers) is the co-legislator with Parliament under Art 294 TFEU. The European Council sets direction but does not legislate, and the Council of Europe is a separate organisation.

questions.q: Which case first established that EU law prevails over later national legislation?
options: Van Gend en Loos (1963)
Costa v ENEL (1964)
Simmenthal (1978)
Factortame (1990)
questions.why: Costa v ENEL established primacy. Van Gend en Loos concerned direct effect; Simmenthal and Factortame developed the consequences of primacy for national courts.

questions.q: A directive's transposition deadline has passed and it has not been implemented. Which claimant can rely on it directly?
options: A shop worker suing her private employer
A consumer suing a private retailer
A teacher employed by a state school suing the local authority
A private company suing a competitor
questions.why: Directives have only vertical direct effect (Marshall, 1986). A local authority running a school is an emanation of the state; the other defendants are private parties.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Brasserie du Pêcheur conditions for state liability?
options: The rule infringed must be intended to confer rights on individuals
The breach must be sufficiently serious
There must be a direct causal link between breach and damage
The state must have acted intentionally or with gross negligence
questions.why: Fault going beyond a sufficiently serious breach cannot be required; Brasserie and Traghetti (2006) reject making liability depend on intent or gross negligence.

questions.q: Under CILFIT (1982), a court of last instance need NOT refer a question of EU law when:
options: The parties agree that no reference is needed
The correct answer is so obvious as to leave no scope for reasonable doubt
The national court thinks a reference would cause delay
A lower court has already interpreted the provision
questions.why: Acte clair is a CILFIT exception. Party agreement, delay and lower court rulings do not relieve a last-instance court of its Art 267(3) obligation.

questions.q: Which case defined measures having equivalent effect to quantitative restrictions as rules capable of hindering trade 'directly or indirectly, actually or potentially'?
options: Cassis de Dijon (1979)
Keck and Mithouard (1993)
Dassonville (1974)
Commission v Italy (trailers) (2009)
questions.why: This is the Dassonville formula. Cassis added mutual recognition and mandatory requirements; Keck carved out selling arrangements; the trailers case added market access.

questions.q: State Q bans the sale of chocolate unless it is packaged in round boxes. Which analysis is correct?
options: It is a selling arrangement outside Art 34 under Keck
It is a product requirement within Art 34 that needs justification
It is a charge having equivalent effect under Art 30
It is lawful because it applies equally to domestic and imported goods
questions.why: Packaging rules concern the product itself, so Keck does not apply. Under Cassis, equally applicable product rules breach Art 34 unless justified (compare Rau v De Smedt, 1982, on cube-shaped margarine packaging).

questions.q: Under Directive 2004/38, an EU citizen acquires a right of permanent residence after:
options: Three months of residence
Three years of employment
Five years of continuous legal residence
Ten years of residence
questions.why: Art 16 grants permanent residence after five years' continuous legal residence. Ten years matters for enhanced protection against expulsion under Art 28(3).

questions.q: Three rival bus operators agree on the fares they will charge. Under Art 101 TFEU, this is best described as:
options: A restriction by object
A vertical agreement exempt under a block exemption
Lawful unless one of them is dominant
An abuse of a dominant position under Art 102
questions.why: Horizontal price-fixing is a classic object restriction, so anti-competitive effects need not be shown. Dominance is irrelevant to Art 101.

questions.q: Since 1 January 2024, the remaining body of retained EU law in the UK has been called:
options: Direct EU legislation
Assimilated law
Withdrawal law
Domesticated EU law
questions.why: The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 renamed retained EU law 'assimilated law' from the start of 2024.

questions.q: Outline the main stages of the ordinary legislative procedure under Art 294 TFEU.
markScheme: The Commission submits a proposal to Parliament and the Council.
Parliament adopts a first-reading position; if the Council approves it, the act is adopted.
Otherwise the Council adopts its own first-reading position, and Parliament has a second reading (absolute majority of component members needed to reject or amend).
If disagreement remains, a Conciliation Committee seeks a joint text, which Parliament and Council must approve at third reading.
questions.modelAnswer: The Commission proposes legislation to Parliament and the Council. Parliament adopts a first-reading position; if the Council approves it, the act is adopted. If not, the Council adopts its own position and sends it to Parliament for a second reading, where Parliament can approve it, or reject or amend it by an absolute majority of its component members. If the Council does not accept Parliament's amendments, a Conciliation Committee of equal numbers from each side tries to agree a joint text, which must then be approved by both institutions at third reading. In practice most files are agreed at first reading after informal trilogues.

questions.q: Distinguish 'direct applicability' from 'direct effect'.
markScheme: Direct applicability means a measure becomes part of national law without national implementing measures (Art 288 TFEU, regulations).
Direct effect means a provision confers rights individuals can enforce in national courts.
Directives are not directly applicable but can be directly effective vertically if clear, precise and unconditional after the deadline (Van Gend en Loos; Ratti).
questions.modelAnswer: Direct applicability describes how a measure enters national law: under Art 288 TFEU regulations apply automatically in every Member State, with no need for national implementation. Direct effect is about enforceability: whether a provision gives individuals rights they can rely on before national courts, which under Van Gend en Loos requires it to be clear, precise and unconditional. The two often overlap but are distinct. Directives are not directly applicable because they need transposition, yet once the deadline has passed they can be directly effective against the state (Ratti; Marshall).

questions.q: Explain the limits of the duty of consistent interpretation.
markScheme: The duty applies only 'as far as possible': no interpretation contra legem (Pupino; Dominguez).
It is limited by general principles of legal certainty and non-retroactivity.
A directive cannot by itself determine or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen; Arcaro).
The full duty begins only after the transposition deadline (Adeneler), though courts must not seriously compromise the directive's aims before then.
questions.modelAnswer: Consistent interpretation requires national courts to read national law in the light of a directive only so far as possible. They need not adopt a reading contra legem, against the clear meaning of national law (Pupino, 2005; Dominguez, 2012). The duty is bounded by legal certainty and non-retroactivity, and in particular a directive cannot, through interpretation alone, create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen, 1987). Timing also matters: the full duty begins when the transposition period expires (Adeneler, 2006), though from the directive's entry into force courts must avoid interpretations that would seriously compromise its result.

questions.q: Which bodies can refer questions under Art 267 TFEU, and when must they refer?
markScheme: Any 'court or tribunal' of a Member State, an autonomous EU concept (Dorsch Consult factors) may refer if a ruling is necessary to give judgment.
Courts against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy must refer (Art 267(3)), subject to the CILFIT exceptions.
questions.modelAnswer: Any court or tribunal of a Member State may refer a question if it considers a ruling necessary to give judgment. Whether a body is a court or tribunal is an EU-law question decided using the Dorsch Consult factors, such as being established by law, permanent and independent. A court against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy under national law must refer, unless one of the CILFIT exceptions applies.

questions.q: Explain how the Commission can secure financial penalties against a Member State under Art 260 TFEU.
markScheme: Art 260(2): if a state fails to comply with an earlier infringement judgment, the Commission can bring it back before the Court after giving it the chance to submit observations.
The Court may impose a lump sum, a periodic penalty, or both together (Commission v France (fishing), 2005).
Art 260(3): where a state fails to notify measures transposing a legislative directive, penalties can be sought in the first Art 258 action.
Interim measures under Art 279 may also carry daily penalties (as against Poland in 2021).
questions.modelAnswer: If a Member State does not comply with a judgment finding an infringement, the Commission can bring a second action under Art 260(2) after giving the state the chance to respond. The Court can then impose a lump sum penalising past non-compliance, a periodic penalty to push future compliance, or both together, as in Commission v France (2005). Art 260(3), added by Lisbon, lets the Commission ask for penalties in the first action where a state has failed to notify measures transposing a legislative directive. Separately, the Court may attach daily penalties to interim orders under Art 279, as it did against Poland in 2021.

questions.q: What is the difference between a 'selling arrangement' and a 'product requirement' after Keck (1993)?
markScheme: Product requirements concern the goods themselves (name, form, size, weight, composition, presentation, labelling, packaging) and fall within Art 34 under Cassis.
Selling arrangements concern how, when, where and by whom goods are sold.
Selling arrangements fall outside Art 34 only if they apply to all relevant traders and affect domestic and imported goods in the same way in law and in fact.
questions.modelAnswer: Product requirements relate to the goods themselves, such as their designation, shape, size, composition, labelling or packaging. Because imports may have to be altered to comply, they fall within Art 34 and need justification under Cassis de Dijon. Selling arrangements govern the circumstances of sale, such as opening hours, who may sell, or advertising. Keck held that these fall outside Art 34 provided they apply to all traders operating in the territory and affect domestic and imported products alike, in law and in fact.

questions.q: Explain how the Court of Justice's approach to social benefits for economically inactive EU citizens has changed.
markScheme: Early case law used citizenship and equal treatment to extend benefits (Martínez Sala, 1998; Grzelczyk, 2001), requiring a degree of financial solidarity.
Baumbast (2002) applied proportionality to the conditions on residence.
Dano (2014) and Alimanovic (2015) tied equal treatment to having a right to reside under Directive 2004/38, so benefits can be refused.
Commission v UK (2016) accepted a right-to-reside test for certain benefits as justified to protect public finances.
questions.modelAnswer: Initially the Court read citizenship expansively. In Grzelczyk (2001) a French student in Belgium could claim a minimum subsistence benefit, the Court speaking of a degree of financial solidarity between nationals of different states, and Baumbast (2002) applied proportionality to residence conditions. From 2014 the approach tightened. Dano and Alimanovic linked equal treatment under Art 24 of Directive 2004/38 to having a lawful right of residence under the Directive, allowing states to refuse benefits to those without one. Commission v UK (2016) accepted the UK's right-to-reside test for child benefit and child tax credit as justified.

questions.q: Explain the difference between freedom of establishment and freedom to provide services.
markScheme: Establishment (Art 49): pursuit of an economic activity through a fixed base in another state on a stable and continuous basis.
Services (Art 56-57): temporary provision across borders for remuneration, residually where other freedoms do not apply.
Gebhard (1995): the temporary nature is assessed by duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity; some infrastructure does not make it establishment.
questions.modelAnswer: Freedom of establishment under Art 49 TFEU covers taking up and pursuing an economic activity on a stable and continuous basis through a fixed base in another Member State, for example opening a branch. Freedom to provide services under Arts 56-57 covers activities provided temporarily across borders for remuneration. Gebhard held that the temporary character of services depends on the duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity of the activity, and that a provider may equip itself with some infrastructure, such as an office, without becoming established.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 on the body of law the UK kept after Brexit.
markScheme: It revoked a scheduled list of retained EU instruments at the end of 2023.
From 1 January 2024 it renamed retained EU law 'assimilated law'.
It abolished the supremacy of retained EU law and removed the general principles of EU law and directly effective rights preserved by s 4 EUWA.
It created ministerial powers to restate, revoke or replace assimilated law, and changed the rules on departing from retained (now 'assimilated') case law.
questions.modelAnswer: The 2023 Act revoked a listed set of retained EU instruments at the end of 2023. From 1 January 2024, it renamed what remained 'assimilated law'. It ended the special status of that law: supremacy no longer applies, the general principles of EU law are no longer part of domestic law, and the directly effective rights preserved by s 4 of the 2018 Act ceased to be recognised. Ministers gained powers to restate, revoke or replace assimilated law by regulations, and the Act revised the test for appellate courts departing from retained (now 'assimilated') CJEU case law and added a mechanism for lower courts to refer such points upwards.

questions.q: 'The European Union's law-making process has a legitimacy problem that the Lisbon Treaty did not solve.' Discuss.
markScheme: Identifies the concept of democratic deficit and its main strands (distance from voters, executive dominance, opacity).
Explains the growth of Parliament's powers culminating in the ordinary legislative procedure as default (Art 294 TFEU).
Notes Parliament's role in electing the Commission President and the Spitzenkandidaten practice and its limits.
Discusses Council transparency and QMV, including the 55%/65% double majority.
Considers the role of national parliaments under Protocols 1 and 2 (yellow and orange cards).
Mentions participatory tools such as the European Citizens' Initiative (Art 11(4) TEU).
Criticises informal trilogues and the dominance of first-reading agreements.
Addresses the Commission's near-monopoly of initiative.
Uses case law on procedural guarantees (Isoglucose; Chernobyl) and legal basis (Tobacco Advertising).
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on whether the deficit remains.
questions.modelAnswer:
The legitimacy critique usually has three strands: decision-makers are far from voters, executives dominate legislation, and the process is opaque. Lisbon addressed each in part.

First, it strengthened Parliament. Co-decision became the ordinary legislative procedure under Art 294 TFEU and now covers most areas, giving Parliament an equal veto with the Council. Parliament elects the Commission President on a proposal from the European Council, which must take the elections into account (Art 17(7) TEU). The Spitzenkandidaten practice tied the presidency to election results in 2014, but its abandonment in 2019 showed how fragile that link is. Parliament's procedural rights are also protected by the Court: Isoglucose (1980) annulled an act adopted without its opinion, and Chernobyl (1990) allowed it to sue to defend its prerogatives.

Second, Lisbon added national parliaments. Protocol No 2 lets them object on subsidiarity grounds through yellow and orange cards, and the Citizens' Initiative in Art 11(4) TEU allows a million citizens to invite a proposal. Both have had modest effect: yellow cards are rare and the Commission can maintain its proposal.

Third, Council voting is clearer. The double majority of 55% of states and 65% of population is easier to understand than weighted votes, and the Council must meet in public when legislating (Art 16(8) TEU).

Problems remain. Most files are settled at first reading after closed trilogues, which limits public scrutiny. The Commission, which is not directly elected, keeps the near-monopoly of initiative. Turnout in European elections remains lower than in most national elections, which weakens Parliament's claim to represent voters. Some scholars, notably Moravcsik, argue the deficit is overstated because the EU's powers are limited by conferral (checked by the Court in Tobacco Advertising, 2000) and because national governments accountable to voters sit in the Council.

On balance, Lisbon improved legitimacy significantly but did not resolve the deeper problem: the absence of a strong European public sphere and continuing opacity in practice.

questions.q: Critically assess the Court of Justice's refusal to give directives horizontal direct effect, and whether the techniques it has developed in its place adequately protect individuals.
markScheme: States the rule in Marshall (1986) and Faccini Dori (1994) and the reasoning based on Art 288 TFEU and the estoppel rationale.
Considers arguments for horizontal effect (Advocate General Jacobs in Vaneetveld; Lenz in Faccini Dori): equality, effectiveness, publication of directives.
Explains the wide concept of state emanation (Foster; Farrell v Whitty) and its arbitrariness.
Analyses indirect effect (Von Colson; Marleasing; Pfeiffer) and its contra legem limit.
Analyses incidental effect (CIA Security; Unilever Italia) and its uncertain boundaries.
Analyses horizontal effect via general principles and the Charter (Mangold; Kücükdeveci; Egenberger; Bauer) and its limits (AMS).
Analyses state liability (Francovich; Brasserie) as a remedy against the state rather than the wrongdoer.
Evaluates legal certainty and the Treaty text against effective protection.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Court has consistently refused to let directives impose obligations on private parties (Marshall, 1986; Faccini Dori, 1994). It rests this on Art 288 TFEU, which addresses directives to Member States, and on an estoppel idea: a state cannot benefit from its own failure to transpose, but a private party has committed no such fault. Legal certainty supports the rule, as individuals should not be bound by measures that were not addressed to them.

The rule has been criticised. Advocates General such as Lenz in Faccini Dori argued that it produces inequality: identical employees get different protection depending on whether their employer is public or private. Since directives must be published in the Official Journal, the legal-certainty objection is weaker.

The Court has softened the rule's effects with four techniques. First, the broad notion of the state in Foster v British Gas (1990) and Farrell v Whitty (2017) brings privatised utilities and insurance bodies within vertical effect, but at the price of arbitrary lines. Second, consistent interpretation (Von Colson; Marleasing; Pfeiffer) is powerful but cannot be used contra legem (Dominguez, 2012) and depends on how willing national courts are to stretch domestic wording. Third, incidental effect (CIA Security; Unilever Italia) lets directives exclude national rules in private disputes, though the line between excluding a rule and imposing an obligation is hard to draw. Fourth, general principles and Charter rights can bind private parties (Mangold; Kücükdeveci; Egenberger; Bauer), but only where the right is sufficient in itself, which the Art 27 consultation right was not (AMS, 2014).

Finally, Francovich and Brasserie liability compensates individuals but sends them against the state, through slower proceedings, and depends on showing a sufficiently serious breach.

The result is a patchwork. It protects individuals more than the bare rule suggests, but at a high cost in complexity and uneven outcomes. A franker acceptance of horizontal effect after the deadline might be simpler, but the Court's caution reflects real concerns about the Treaty text and the limits of its own legitimacy.

questions.q: 'Supremacy of EU law is accepted absolutely by the Court of Justice but only conditionally by national courts. This tension is both inevitable and productive.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the CJEU's absolute claim: Costa, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Simmenthal, Factortame.
Notes the Lisbon Declaration 17 and the failure to write primacy into the Treaties.
Analyses the German Constitutional Court: Solange I and II, Maastricht, Lisbon, Honeywell, and Weiss (PSPP, 2020).
Considers other national courts (Italian Taricco saga, Danish Ajos, Czech Landtová).
Discusses Poland's K 3/21 (2021) and the rule-of-law dimension, plus the Commission's infringement response.
Explains Art 4(2) TEU national identity as a mediating tool (Sayn-Wittgenstein; Taricco II/M.A.S.).
Engages with constitutional pluralism theory (MacCormick, Walker, Kumm) versus critics.
Evaluates whether the dialogue has produced improvements (fundamental rights protection; limits on ultra vires).
Considers whether Poland shows that the tension can become destructive.
Mentions the UK's own position before Brexit (Factortame; HS2; Miller) as illustration.
Reaches a nuanced conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Court of Justice treats primacy as unconditional. Costa v ENEL (1964) grounded it in the transfer of sovereignty; Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (1970) extended it over national constitutions; Simmenthal (1978) required every court to disapply conflicting law. Yet primacy was never written into the Treaties, appearing only in Declaration 17 to Lisbon, and national constitutional courts have often derived EU law's authority from their own constitutions rather than from the Treaties.

The German Federal Constitutional Court is the clearest example. Solange I (1974) reserved fundamental-rights review; Solange II (1986) suspended it while EU protection remained broadly equivalent. Maastricht and Lisbon developed ultra vires and constitutional identity review, Honeywell (2010) limited ultra vires findings to manifest and structurally significant transfers, and Weiss (2020) used the doctrine for the first time, declaring the CJEU's ruling on the ECB's bond purchases incomprehensible. Czech (Landtová, 2012) and Danish (Ajos, 2016) courts have also refused to follow CJEU rulings.

Is the tension productive? Constitutional pluralists such as MacCormick and Walker argue that the absence of a final arbiter forces courts into dialogue. There is evidence: Solange pushed the Court to develop fundamental rights as general principles, eventually leading to the Charter. The Taricco saga shows the CJEU retreating in M.A.S. (2017) after the Italian Constitutional Court invoked counter-limits. Art 4(2) TEU on national identity lets the Court accommodate national concerns (Sayn-Wittgenstein, 2010).

But the tension has a darker side. The Polish Constitutional Tribunal's K 3/21 (2021) borrowed the language of identity and ultra vires to shield measures undermining judicial independence. The Commission responded with infringement proceedings. This suggests that conditional acceptance is productive only between courts committed to shared values; when a captured court invokes it, pluralism becomes cover for defiance.

Before Brexit, UK courts likewise treated supremacy as statutory (HS2, 2014; Miller, 2017).

The tension is inevitable in a non-federal order built on national constitutions. It has been productive where dialogue is in good faith, improving rights protection and checking competence creep, but it is dangerous when used to escape the rule of law. Its value therefore depends on who invokes it and why.

questions.q: The (fictional) Workplace Noise Directive required Member States to ensure, by 1 March 2024, that employers provide ear protection and compensate workers who suffer hearing loss through failure to do so. The Member State of Freedonia has done nothing to transpose it. Priya works at Loudco Ltd, a private factory, and Sam works at a hospital run by the Freedonian Health Authority. Both suffered hearing loss in 2025 because no protection was provided. Advise Priya and Sam on whether and how they can rely on the Directive.
markScheme: Identifies that the deadline has passed so direct effect is possible (Ratti).
Applies the Van Gend en Loos criteria to the provisions.
Sam: the Health Authority is an emanation of the state (Foster; Farrell v Whitty) so vertical direct effect available (Marshall).
Priya: no horizontal direct effect against Loudco (Marshall; Faccini Dori).
Priya: indirect effect requires existing national law that can be interpreted consistently (Marleasing; Pfeiffer), limited by contra legem.
Considers whether any general principle or Charter right could apply horizontally (Art 31(1) Charter fair working conditions; uncertain).
Francovich/Brasserie liability: rights conferred, identifiable content, causation.
Non-transposition is sufficiently serious per se (Dillenkofer).
Notes national procedural autonomy subject to equivalence and effectiveness.
Clear conclusions for each claimant.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both claims arise after the 1 March 2024 deadline, so the Directive can in principle have direct effect (Ratti, 1979). Its obligations appear clear, precise and unconditional (Van Gend en Loos).

Sam. Sam's employer is a public health authority. Directives can be enforced vertically against the state and its emanations (Marshall, 1986), and Farrell v Whitty (2017) confirms that a body entrusted by the state with a public-interest task and given special powers qualifies. A state health authority clearly does. Sam can rely directly on the Directive in the Freedonian courts against the Authority.

Priya. Loudco is a private company, and directives cannot impose obligations on private parties (Marshall; Faccini Dori, 1994). Priya has three alternatives.

First, indirect effect. Freedonian courts must interpret any relevant national law, such as general employer health and safety or negligence rules, as far as possible in line with the Directive (Von Colson; Marleasing, 1990), considering the whole body of national law (Pfeiffer, 2004). If an existing duty of care or safety statute can be read to require ear protection and compensation, she may succeed against Loudco. But a court cannot read national law contra legem (Dominguez, 2012), so if domestic law clearly excludes such liability this route fails.

Second, she might argue that a Charter right applies horizontally. Art 31(1) protects working conditions that respect health and safety, but unlike the paid-leave right in Bauer (2018) it is probably too general to be enforced between private parties on its own. This argument is weak.

Third, state liability. Under Francovich and Brasserie du Pêcheur, the Directive is intended to confer rights on workers, their content is identifiable, and complete failure to transpose is a sufficiently serious breach per se (Dillenkofer, 1996). If her loss results directly from the absence of protection that transposition would have required, Freedonia must compensate her.

Conclusion: Sam can sue the Authority directly; Priya should argue consistent interpretation against Loudco and, failing that, sue Freedonia for damages.

questions.q: 'State liability under Francovich was meant to complete the system of judicial protection; in practice it is too uncertain to do so.' Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Explains the rationale of Francovich (1991): effectiveness and Art 4(3) TEU.
Sets out Brasserie du Pêcheur and Factortame (No 3) conditions and the parallel with Art 340 non-contractual liability (Bergaderm).
Analyses 'sufficiently serious' and its factors.
Contrasts Dillenkofer and Hedley Lomas with ex p British Telecommunications and Denkavit.
Discusses judicial liability (Köbler; Traghetti) and its rarity in practice (Köbler itself failing on the facts).
Discusses causation and its delegation to national courts.
Addresses national procedural autonomy, equivalence and effectiveness, and the risk of divergent outcomes.
Uses the UK experience (Factortame (No 5) in the House of Lords, 1999) to show the test working.
Considers the relationship with direct and indirect effect: liability as a fall-back.
Considers whether more precise rules would undermine flexibility.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Francovich (1991) held that the full effectiveness of EU law would be impaired if individuals could not obtain redress when a state's breach caused them loss, grounding liability in the Treaty system and in the duty of sincere cooperation. It filled gaps left by the lack of horizontal direct effect and by weak public enforcement.

Brasserie du Pêcheur and Factortame (No 3) (1996) aligned state liability with the Union's own liability under Art 340 TFEU, a link later confirmed in Bergaderm (2000). The test has three conditions, of which the second, a sufficiently serious breach, carries most of the uncertainty.

Clear cases exist. Complete non-transposition is serious per se (Dillenkofer, 1996); where the state has little or no discretion, mere infringement may suffice (Hedley Lomas, 1996). Conversely, an excusable error about an unclear directive defeats liability (ex p British Telecommunications, 1996; Denkavit, 1996). Between these lie many hard cases, and the list of factors from Brasserie gives national courts a broad evaluative discretion.

This uncertainty is greatest for judicial breaches. Köbler (2003) extended liability to last-instance courts, but required a manifest infringement and on the facts found none. Traghetti (2006) prevented states from confining such liability to intent or gross negligence, yet successful claims remain rare. Causation and quantum are left to national courts, applying national procedures subject to equivalence and effectiveness, which inevitably produces divergence between Member States.

On the other hand, the regime has worked when needed. In Factortame (No 5) (1999) the House of Lords held the UK's breaches of the fishing rules sufficiently serious, the legislation being manifestly discriminatory on grounds of nationality. Uncertainty also serves a purpose: a rigid rule would either expose states to liability for every misreading or excuse serious defiance.

The statement is partly right. State liability is an imperfect remedy: it is litigated against the state rather than the wrongdoer, costly, slow and fact-sensitive. But it was never meant to stand alone. It works alongside direct effect, consistent interpretation and infringement proceedings, and as a backstop for serious failures it does complete the system, if unevenly.

questions.q: Orsino is a tribunal in the fictional Member State of Lavoria, set up by statute to decide disputes about public procurement. Its members are appointed by the Minister for a renewable two-year term and can be removed by the Minister without cause. A dispute before it turns on the interpretation of an EU procurement directive. Its decisions can be appealed only with permission to the Lavorian Supreme Court, which has refused permission in every procurement case for five years. Separately, Tancredi argues before Orsino that the directive itself is invalid because it was adopted on the wrong legal basis. Advise Orsino on whether it may or must refer, and how it should deal with Tancredi's argument.
markScheme: Explains the Art 267 framework and the autonomous concept of 'court or tribunal'.
Applies Dorsch Consult factors: established by law, permanent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes, rules of law.
Focuses on independence: removal without cause and ministerial control (Wilson, 2006; Banco de Santander, 2020).
Concludes Orsino is probably not a court or tribunal and cannot refer.
In the alternative, considers whether it is a court of last instance (Lyckeskog): appeal with leave means it is not.
Notes the practical refusal pattern does not change Lyckeskog, though the Supreme Court would then be bound to refer when deciding on leave.
Discusses CILFIT exceptions and Consorzio.
On validity: national courts cannot declare EU acts invalid (Foto-Frost) and may need to refer.
Interim relief possibility (Zuckerfabrik; Atlanta).
Notes Tancredi may be barred if he could clearly have brought a direct action (TWD Textilwerke).
Clear advice.
questions.modelAnswer:
Can Orsino refer? Only a 'court or tribunal' may refer under Art 267, an autonomous EU concept assessed using the Dorsch Consult (1997) factors. Orsino is statutory, permanent, compulsory, inter partes and applies rules of law. The difficulty is independence. The Court requires protection against external intervention, including guarantees about appointment and removal (Wilson, 2006). In Banco de Santander (2020) the Court refused a reference from a Spanish tax body whose members could be removed without adequate safeguards. Orsino's members can be dismissed by the Minister without cause and serve short renewable terms at ministerial discretion. On that basis Orsino probably fails the independence requirement and cannot refer.

If Orsino were a court or tribunal, it would have a discretion under Art 267(2), not an obligation. Under Lyckeskog (2002), a body whose decisions may be appealed to a supreme court with permission is not a court of last instance, because the supreme court must itself refer at the leave stage if needed. The Supreme Court's consistent refusals do not change this in law, although they could found a Köbler claim against Lavoria if the Supreme Court repeatedly fails to refer where it should. Even a last-instance court could rely on the CILFIT exceptions, but Consorzio Italian Management (2021) makes acte clair demanding.

Tancredi's argument. No national court may declare an EU act invalid (Foto-Frost, 1987). If Orsino regards the challenge as unfounded, it may reject it and apply the directive. If it has serious doubts, the proper course is a reference on validity; if Orsino cannot refer, Tancredi must take the point to a body that can, usually on appeal. Interim relief is available only on the strict Zuckerfabrik (1991) conditions. Tancredi may also be barred if he had undoubted standing to challenge the directive directly under Art 263 within two months and failed to do so (TWD Textilwerke, 1994), which is unlikely for a directive.

Advice: Orsino should decline to refer for lack of independence, and decide the interpretive point itself. On Tancredi's point, it may reject the challenge and apply the directive if it considers it unfounded, but it cannot declare the directive invalid; if it has serious doubts, the point must be taken on appeal to a court that can refer.

questions.q: The fictional Member State of Arbrea passes three measures: (a) a law requiring all cheese sold in Arbrea to contain at least 50% Arbrean milk, (b) a ban on selling any alcohol between 10pm and 8am, and (c) a ban on advertising craft beer on television, aimed at reducing youth drinking. Kees, a Dutch exporter of cheese and craft beer, wants to know whether these measures breach EU law.
markScheme: Identifies Art 34 TFEU and the Dassonville formula.
(a) is distinctly applicable/directly discriminatory (Buy Irish), justifiable only under Art 36.
(a) favours domestic producers; economic aims cannot justify it; likely unlawful.
(b) is a selling arrangement (Keck): applies to all traders and affects all products equally; outside Art 34.
(c) is a selling arrangement but may fail the 'in fact' limb (Gourmet; De Agostini) because imports rely more on advertising.
(c) if within Art 34, justification on public health under Art 36 or mandatory requirements.
Proportionality analysis for (c): suitability and necessity; selective ban on craft beer raises consistency concerns.
Notes possible arbitrary discrimination if domestic beers are largely mainstream.
Clear conclusion on each measure.
questions.modelAnswer:
All three measures concern trade in goods, so Art 34 TFEU applies. Under Dassonville (1974), any national rule capable of hindering trade between Member States directly or indirectly, actually or potentially, is a measure having equivalent effect to a quantitative restriction.

(a) Domestic milk requirement. Requiring cheese to contain Arbrean milk directly favours domestic produce over imports, like the Buy Irish campaign (1982). It is a distinctly applicable measure. Such measures can be justified only under Art 36, not by the Cassis mandatory requirements. Arbrea's evident aim is to protect its dairy farmers, an economic objective that can never justify a restriction. Even if Arbrea claimed health or quality reasons, these could be met by labelling and do not depend on the milk's national origin. Measure (a) breaches Art 34.

(b) Night-time alcohol sales ban. A rule on when goods may be sold is a classic selling arrangement under Keck (1993). It applies to all traders in Arbrea and affects Arbrean and imported alcohol in the same way in law and in fact. It therefore falls outside Art 34. Even if it did not, public health would readily justify it.

(c) Television advertising ban on craft beer. Advertising rules are selling arrangements, but Gourmet (2001) shows that a ban can fail Keck's second condition if it makes market access harder for imports, which depend on advertising to reach consumers familiar with domestic products.
