If Kees's beer is new to Arbrean consumers, the ban probably affects imports more in fact and falls within Art 34.

It may still be justified on public health grounds under Art 36. Reducing youth drinking is legitimate. However, the measure must be suitable and consistent. Targeting only craft beer, while leaving mainstream beers and spirits free to advertise, undermines its coherence and may suggest disguised protection if Arbrean breweries mostly make mainstream beer. Less restrictive alternatives, such as limits on timing or content, may suffice. The ban is probably disproportionate.

Conclusion: (a) is unlawful; (b) is lawful; (c) likely breaches Art 34 unless Arbrea can produce evidence that a targeted ban is coherent and necessary.

questions.q: 'The Court of Justice has never settled on a single test for what counts as a restriction on the free movement of goods, and the result is an incoherent body of law.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Dassonville's breadth and its potential to catch any regulation.
Explains Cassis de Dijon: mutual recognition and mandatory requirements; dual burden rationale.
Explains the Sunday trading litigation (Torfaen) and overreach that prompted Keck.
Analyses Keck's distinction and criticisms (formalism, difficulty of categorisation).
Discusses post-Keck refinements: Gourmet, DocMorris, De Agostini.
Analyses the market-access cases: Italian trailers, Mickelsson and Roos, and the three-limb restatement.
Compares with the market-access approach in persons and services (Bosman, Alpine Investments) and the convergence debate.
Notes AG Jacobs' substantial-impact proposal in Leclerc-Siplec.
Considers exports (Groenveld; Gysbrechts).
Evaluates whether incoherence is real or tolerable, citing academic views (Weatherill, Barnard, Snell).
Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dassonville (1974) defined measures having equivalent effect so broadly that almost any regulation could be caught. Cassis de Dijon (1979) confirmed that equally applicable rules may restrict trade, especially where they impose a dual burden on imports already compliant with home-state rules.

The breadth of Dassonville led traders to challenge rules with no real cross-border dimension, notably in the Sunday trading cases (Torfaen, 1989). Keck (1993) responded by placing selling arrangements outside Art 34 if they apply to all traders and affect domestic and imported goods alike in law and in fact. Keck brought certainty in many cases but was criticised as formalistic. Advocate General Jacobs in Leclerc-Siplec (1995) argued instead for a test of substantial restriction on market access. The categories of product rule and selling arrangement are not always easy to apply, and the second Keck condition reopened the door: in Gourmet (2001) an advertising ban failed it, and in DocMorris (2003) a ban on internet pharmacy sales did.

The Court then added a third category. In Commission v Italy (trailers, 2009) and Mickelsson and Roos (2009) rules restricting how products could be used were measured by their effect on market access. The trailers judgment restated the law in three limbs: discriminatory measures, Cassis product rules, and any other measure hindering access to the market. This arguably makes market access the unifying idea, aligning goods with persons and services, where Bosman (1995) and Alpine Investments (1995) had already used it.

Is the result incoherent? Some commentators, such as Snell, argue that market access is too vague to guide courts, while others see the three-limb test as reasonably settled.

My view is that the law is more coherent in its principles than in its formulas. Throughout, the Court seeks to catch measures that partition the market or burden cross-border trade disproportionately, while leaving general regulation to the states. The problem is that it expresses this through overlapping tests rather than a single statement. Greater candour that market access is the governing idea, with Keck as a presumption, would improve clarity.

questions.q: Lukas, a German national, moved to the fictional Member State of Hibernia in January 2023. He worked full-time as a chef for 14 months, then was made redundant and registered as a jobseeker. In 2025 he was convicted of a minor assault and fined. His Brazilian wife, Ana, joined him in 2024. Hibernia has refused Lukas jobseeker's allowance and plans to deport both of them on public policy grounds. Advise Lukas and Ana.
markScheme: Lukas was a worker under Art 45 TFEU (Lawrie-Blum).
Art 7(3)(b) Directive 2004/38: involuntary unemployment after more than a year of work, registered as jobseeker, retains worker status.
Retained worker status gives equal treatment in social advantages, so refusal of allowance likely unlawful (Art 24; Reg 492/2011 Art 7(2)).
Contrasts with those who are only jobseekers, including people whose retained status has lapsed (Alimanovic, Art 24(2)).
Ana is a family member (spouse, Art 2(2)(a)) with derived rights; no prior lawful residence required (Metock).
Expulsion requires personal conduct presenting a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat (Art 27(2); Bouchereau).
A previous conviction alone is insufficient; a minor fine unlikely to meet the threshold.
Proportionality factors under Art 28(1) (length of residence, integration).
Ana cannot be expelled on the basis of Lukas's conduct; personal conduct requirement.
Procedural safeguards (Arts 30-31).
Clear conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lukas's status. Working full-time as a chef for 14 months, Lukas was clearly a worker under Art 45 TFEU (Lawrie-Blum, 1986). Under Art 7(3)(b) of Directive 2004/38, a worker who becomes involuntarily unemployed after more than one year of employment and registers as a jobseeker retains worker status. Lukas was made redundant, which is involuntary, after 14 months, and has registered. He therefore keeps worker status.

Jobseeker's allowance. As a person with retained worker status, Lukas is entitled to equal treatment with Hibernian nationals under Art 24 of the Directive and Art 7(2) of Regulation 492/2011, which covers social advantages. The derogation in Art 24(2), allowing refusal of social assistance to jobseekers, applies to those who are only jobseekers, not to those who retain worker status. In Alimanovic (2015) the claimants had worked for less than a year, so their retained status lasted only six months under Art 7(3)(c) and had expired. The refusal is probably unlawful.

Ana's position. As Lukas's spouse, Ana is a family member under Art 2(2)(a) and has a derived right to reside with him. Her Brazilian nationality and lack of prior residence in another Member State are irrelevant (Metock, 2008).

Deportation. Under Art 27(2), expulsion on public policy grounds must be proportionate and based exclusively on the personal conduct of the individual, which must represent a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society (Bouchereau, 1977). Previous criminal convictions do not in themselves justify expulsion. A single minor assault punished by a fine is unlikely to show a present threat. Lukas has not yet acquired permanent residence (fewer than five years), so the ordinary threshold applies, but Art 28(1) still requires Hibernia to weigh his length of residence, integration, family situation and ties to Germany.

Ana has committed no offence. Because measures must be based on personal conduct, she cannot be expelled simply because of Lukas's conviction; and if his expulsion is unlawful, her derived right continues.

Both may challenge any decision through the procedural safeguards in Arts 30-31, including written reasons and access to judicial redress.

Conclusion: Lukas should receive the allowance, and neither can lawfully be deported on these facts.

questions.q: 'EU citizenship was supposed to become the fundamental status of nationals of the Member States. The Court's case law since 2014 has reduced it to a status for the economically active and the self-sufficient.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Arts 20-21 TFEU and the 'fundamental status' phrase from Grzelczyk (2001).
Discusses early expansive cases: Martínez Sala, Grzelczyk, Baumbast, Bidar.
Analyses Directive 2004/38 as framework and the conditions for the inactive.
Analyses Dano (2014), Alimanovic (2015), García-Nieto (2016) and Commission v UK (2016).
Explains the shift to the Directive as the yardstick and abandonment of individual proportionality assessment in Alimanovic.
Considers political context (UK referendum, welfare tourism concerns).
Discusses Zambrano and its narrowing (McCarthy, Dereci) and revival (Chavez-Vilchez).
Considers continuing protection in non-financial areas (Coman; Rottmann; Tjebbes; family reunification).
Considers CG v Department for Communities (2021) and the Charter's role.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
In Grzelczyk (2001) the Court said that Union citizenship is destined to be the fundamental status of Member State nationals. Early cases used Arts 18 and 21 TFEU to extend equal treatment beyond workers: Martínez Sala (1998) and Grzelczyk gave benefits to residents lawfully present; Baumbast (2002) applied proportionality so that a minor shortfall in sickness insurance did not defeat residence; and Bidar (2005) allowed students with a genuine link to claim maintenance support.

Directive 2004/38 codified these rights but also their limits. After three months, inactive citizens need sufficient resources and comprehensive sickness insurance (Art 7(1)(b)), and Art 24(2) allows refusal of social assistance to jobseekers and student support before permanent residence.

From 2014 the Court treated the Directive as the decisive yardstick. In Dano (2014) an inactive Romanian national in Germany without resources had no right to reside under the Directive and so could not claim equal treatment. Alimanovic (2015) held that no individual assessment of proportionality was required where the Directive's graduated scheme already took account of personal circumstances. García-Nieto (2016) and Commission v UK (2016) went further, accepting a right-to-reside test for certain benefits.

The statement captures this shift in social-welfare law. The inactive and poor now have limited protection from citizenship alone. Even CG v Department for Communities (2021), which invoked the Charter, required only that the host state ensure a dignified existence for a vulnerable mother and children rather than restoring full equal treatment.

But citizenship is more than access to benefits. In non-financial areas the Court remains protective. Zambrano (2011) protects the substance of citizenship rights; though narrowed in McCarthy and Dereci (2011), it was revived in Chavez-Vilchez (2017). Rottmann (2010) and Tjebbes (2019) subject loss of nationality to proportionality review, and Coman (2018) protects same-sex spouses.

The more accurate conclusion is that citizenship is a full status for mobility, family life and identity, but a conditional one for welfare. The statement overstates the decline, though it is right that the 'fundamental status' promise has not been fulfilled for the economically inactive.

questions.q: Fitbox is a gym chain incorporated in the fictional Member State of Norland, where company law is light. It has no operations there and runs all its gyms in Solaria. Solaria requires branches of foreign companies to have minimum share capital of €50,000, which Fitbox does not. Separately, Fitbox holds 65% of the Solarian market for gym services and offers members large discounts if they cancel memberships with other chains. Its two main competitors have agreed with each other not to open gyms within two kilometres of each other's sites. Advise on the legality of these arrangements under EU law.
markScheme: Identifies Art 49/54 TFEU and Centros (1999); registering abroad is legitimate use of freedom.
Applies Inspire Art (2003): extra requirements on foreign companies are restrictions.
Gebhard justification: creditor protection unlikely to be suitable/proportionate where creditors know company is foreign.
Abuse only where wholly artificial/fraudulent, not mere choice of law.
Art 102: market definition (gym services in Solaria) and dominance (65%, AKZO presumption, United Brands).
Exclusivity-inducing discounts as potential abuse (Hoffmann-La Roche; Intel effects analysis and as-efficient competitor).
Objective justification/efficiency defence.
Competitors' agreement: Art 101 market-sharing, restriction by object (Cartes Bancaires).
Effect on trade between Member States; local market issue.
Art 101(3) unlikely; voidness (Art 101(2)) and fines.
Clear conclusions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Establishment. Fitbox chose Norland for its light company law and trades entirely through Solaria. Under Arts 49 and 54 TFEU, companies formed under the law of a Member State enjoy freedom of establishment. In Centros (1999) the Court held that registering in a state with lighter requirements to trade through a branch elsewhere is not in itself an abuse. Solaria's minimum capital rule for foreign branches is a restriction: it imposes conditions on Fitbox that its home law does not, exactly as in Inspire Art (2003).

Solaria may try to justify it under the Gebhard test as protecting creditors. Centros rejected that argument: creditors are on notice that Fitbox is governed by Norland law, and alternative measures could protect them. Solaria could act only against genuine fraud, such as using foreign incorporation to evade debts. The rule is probably unlawful.

Fitbox's discounts. The relevant market is likely gym services in Solaria. A 65% share raises a presumption of dominance (AKZO, 1991), reinforced if competitors are much smaller, so Fitbox has the power to act independently in the United Brands sense. Discounts conditional on members leaving rivals operate like exclusivity rebates. Hoffmann-La Roche (1979) treated loyalty rebates by a dominant firm as abusive, but Intel (2017) requires the Commission or court to examine evidence submitted by the dominant firm that the conduct cannot foreclose an as-efficient competitor. Fitbox may argue that discounts are ordinary price competition. If they are targeted at rivals' customers and priced so that rivals cannot match them, abuse under Art 102 is likely.

Competitors' agreement. Two rival chains agreeing not to open near each other's sites is a market-sharing agreement, a restriction by object under Art 101(1) (Cartes Bancaires, 2014). It is appreciable by nature (Expedia, 2012). An effect on inter-state trade must be shown, which may be hard for a local market; otherwise national competition law applies. If Art 101 applies, the agreement is void (Art 101(2)) and practically incapable of exemption under Art 101(3).

Conclusion: Solaria's capital rule breaches Art 49; Fitbox's discounts risk abusing dominance; the rivals' agreement is likely unlawful market-sharing.

questions.q: In 2026, Rhiannon, a care worker in Cardiff, claims that her private employer has denied her holiday pay rights derived from the Working Time Directive. She relies on (i) a 2018 CJEU judgment interpreting the Directive, (ii) a 2025 CJEU judgment extending that interpretation, (iii) the general principle of effectiveness, and (iv) Art 31(2) of the Charter. Advise her on how a UK court is likely to treat each argument.
markScheme: Outlines EUWA 2018, end of implementation period, and REULA 2023 assimilated law.
Working Time Regulations 1998 as assimilated law; note 2023 amendments to holiday pay rules (Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023).
(i) Pre-2021 CJEU case law, now 'assimilated case law', binds lower courts (s 6 EUWA) unless departed from by appellate courts or modified by legislation.
Notes tribunals/High Court bound; Court of Appeal/Supreme Court may depart applying the test as amended in 2023.
(ii) Post-2020 CJEU rulings are not binding; court 'may have regard' (s 6(2)).
(iii) General principles no longer part of domestic law for events after 2023 (REULA 2023).
(iv) Charter not part of domestic law (s 5(4) EUWA); Bauer horizontal effect unavailable.
No supremacy of assimilated law over later domestic legislation; interpretation now in line with domestic statute.
Alternative routes: domestic statutory construction, Employment Rights Act, Human Rights Act limited.
Northern Ireland/Withdrawal Agreement routes inapplicable to Wales.
Clear conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Rhiannon's claim arises in Wales in 2026, after both the end of the implementation period on 31 December 2020 and the reforms of the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023. The Working Time Regulations 1998, which implemented the Directive, continue as assimilated law, as amended by the 2023 regulations that restated certain holiday pay rules. Her rights must therefore be found in that domestic text.

(i) The 2018 CJEU judgment. Under s 6 of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, as amended, CJEU case law handed down before the end of 2020 remains binding as 'assimilated case law' (called retained case law until 2024), binding on employment tribunals and the High Court unless modified by legislation. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court may depart from it, applying the factors added in 2023. Unless Parliament has altered the relevant provision, a tribunal will follow the 2018 interpretation in reading the Regulations. This is her strongest argument.

(ii) The 2025 CJEU judgment. Post-2020 CJEU decisions do not bind UK courts, though under s 6(2) a court may have regard to them so far as relevant. A tribunal may find it persuasive but cannot be required to follow it, especially if it extends the law beyond what the Regulations' wording supports.

(iii) The general principle of effectiveness. The 2023 Act removed the general principles of EU law from domestic law for events after 2023. Rhiannon cannot rely on effectiveness to disapply or stretch the Regulations.

(iv) Art 31(2) of the Charter. The Charter ceased to be part of domestic law at exit (s 5(4) EUWA). The horizontal effect recognised in Bauer (2018) is therefore unavailable against her private employer.

Further, assimilated law no longer enjoys supremacy, so it cannot override other domestic legislation.

Advice: Rhiannon should frame her claim under the Regulations as interpreted by pre-2021 case law, citing the 2025 judgment as persuasive, and not rely on general principles or the Charter. Her success will depend on whether the 2023 amendments changed the specific provision she relies on.

questions.q: Explain how the Court of Justice's approach to loyalty rebates under Art 102 TFEU changed in Intel (2017).
markScheme: Hoffmann-La Roche (1979) treated exclusivity rebates by a dominant undertaking as abusive in themselves, a near per se approach.
Intel (2017) confirmed that starting point but held that where the dominant firm submits evidence that its conduct could not restrict competition, the Commission must examine it.
The assessment considers the extent of dominance, the share of the market covered, the conditions and duration of the rebates, and any strategy to exclude as-efficient competitors.
The as-efficient competitor test becomes relevant, and efficiencies may justify the conduct; this marks a shift towards an effects-based approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Under Hoffmann-La Roche (1979), rebates conditional on a customer obtaining all or most of its needs from a dominant supplier were abusive almost automatically, because they tie customers and deny rivals access. Intel (2017) kept that presumption but qualified it. If the dominant firm submits evidence, during the administrative procedure, that its rebates could not foreclose competitors, the Commission must analyse the extent of the firm's dominance, the share of the market covered, the conditions and duration of the rebates, and whether they could exclude an as-efficient competitor. Efficiency benefits may outweigh harm. The case moved Art 102 towards an effects-based approach.
